title: 0/1 Knapsack
tagline: Take it or leave it — the template behind subset-sum, partition, and budget problems.

intuition.analogy: A thief with a weight-limited bag faces each item once: grab it (gain its value, lose its weight capacity) or skip it. The best haul is the better of those two choices, computed for every capacity.
paragraphs: 0/1 knapsack maximises total value of chosen items without exceeding a weight capacity W, where each item is taken at most once. The core decision for each item is binary: include or exclude.
Define dp[i][w] = best value using the first i items with capacity w. Either you skip item i (dp[i-1][w]) or take it if it fits (dp[i-1][w-wt[i]] + val[i]). The maximum of those is the answer.

Because each cell only depends on the previous row, you can compress to a 1D array — but you must iterate capacity from high to low so each item is used once (low-to-high would allow reusing it, which is the unbounded knapsack).
intuition.keyIdea: For each item, dp[w] = max(skip = dp[w], take = dp[w − wt] + val). Iterate w downward for the 0/1 version.

steps.title: Define the state
steps.detail: dp[w] = best value achievable with capacity w using the items processed so far.

steps.title: Process items one by one
steps.detail: For each item, update dp[w] for w from W down to wt: dp[w] = max(dp[w], dp[w-wt] + val).

steps.title: Read the answer
steps.detail: dp[W] holds the maximum value within the capacity.

complexity.timeReason: n items times W capacities. 'Pseudo-polynomial' since it depends on the numeric value W, not its bit length.

pitfalls: Iterate capacity downward for 0/1; upward turns it into unbounded knapsack.
Pseudo-polynomial: huge W makes it impractical — sometimes you DP on value instead.
Initialise dp correctly: 0 for 'max value' problems; ∞/−∞ for 'exact'/'minimum' variants.

dryRun.clickMoment: At w=4 after item 2, dp becomes 35 (items 1+2). Item 3 alone is only 30, so the table correctly keeps the better combination — each cell remembers the best of all decisions so far.

problems.title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
problems.statement: Can the array be split into two equal-sum subsets?

approach: If the total is odd it can't split evenly. Otherwise ask: can a subset sum to total/2? That's a 0/1 subset-sum knapsack.
Boolean dp over reachable sums; iterate sums downward so each number is used at most once.

problems.title: Target Sum
problems.statement: Count ways to assign +/- to reach a target.
problems.hint: Transform to a subset-sum counting knapsack.

approach: Splitting numbers into + and - groups with sum S means the positive group sums to (total + S)/2. Count subsets reaching that target.
Check feasibility (non-negative, even). Then a counting subset-sum knapsack: dp[s] += dp[s-x] iterating downward.

problems.title: Last Stone Weight II
problems.hint: Partition into two groups as balanced as possible — subset sum.

approach: Smashing stones with signs ±1 leaves total - 2·(subset sum). To minimise the residue, maximise a subset sum not exceeding total/2.
Subset-sum knapsack over reachable sums; the answer is total - 2·bestReachable.

problems.title: Coin Change
problems.statement: Fewest coins to make an amount.

approach: Coins are reusable, so this is the unbounded-knapsack variant: dp[a] = fewest coins for amount a.
Iterate the amount upward for each coin so a coin can be picked multiple times.

approach: Two capacities: members used and minimum profit reached. dp[g][p] = number of schemes using g members achieving at least p profit.
For each crime add a dimension and iterate members downward (0/1). Cap profit at minProfit so all higher profits collapse into one bucket. Sum over all g.
